newsitem.title: USA: Boz the bull riding high at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Boz the bull riding high at G7 summit.

text.p: Boz the bull was supposed to be a relatively tame critter, suitable for showing, but he turned mean and was killed, stuffed and now has a role at the Denver summit of industrialised nations.
Boz has been set up in the summit press area at the Colorado Convention Centre, where reporters were lining up to put on a cowboy hat and sit astride the beast for a photograph.
Boz was arranged to look like he was kicking his back legs high into the air, against the backdrop of a rodeo scene.
The beast was the product of Colorado cowboy and metal worker Willis Hamm, said Ken Gerbrandt, who is in charge of the exhibit.

"This particular bull, Willis Hamm wanted to train it for pictures, for show, but after a couple of years, it became mean. His temperament was not right for that work, and so he became food for the poor. He was stuffed and has been in storage for three years," said the cowboy-hatted Gerbrandt.
Boz was one of the few examples of old Western heritage on display at the convention centre. Most of the exhibits were high technology, in keeping with Denver's more modern profile.
There was even a virtual reality display of knee surgery.
Perhaps the most relaxing fare was the summit massage station.

Anni Bade (slogan - "Hands to Heal the World"), Terri Duran (specialities: Swedish and Deep Tissue) and a team of eager masseuses are busy rubbing away the pain of members of the international media covering the summit.

"The two stress points we're expecting most trouble with are the suboccipital muscles and the superior angle of the scapula," one masseuse, Nancy Wall, helfully explained, referring to the neck and shoulder blade area.

Contributing to the problem were the stress of looming deadlines, heavy camera equipment, the Rocky Mountain city's high altitude and dry atmosphere that causes dehydration, and the hard concrete floor of the press centre.
"Stress creates an attitude," said Bade, adding that the Denver summit has all the mental, emotional and physical ingredients for back and neck problems.
Does it take any extra skills to handle the members of the media? "Not really," said Bade. "A butt is a butt."

In keeping with the lofty tone of the occasion, even the graffiti in the press centre toilets have a high-minded tone. On otherwise shiny clean walls some earnest scribe has written: "Stop all foreign aid and help the homeless."
Out at The Fort restaurant in nearby Morrison, owner Sam Arnold is happily preparing his place for a "19th century cookout" on Saturday night for the summit participants.
"I'm tickled to death," he said.
Arnold serves up a gastronomical array including rattlesnake, buffalo tongue, broiled buffalo bone marrow and deep-fried "Rocky Mountain oysters" -- which are animal testicles.
But it was not clear if President Bill Clinton, Russian President Boris Yeltsin and their summit colleagues would be dining on this fare.
Arnold said White House chefs have essentially taken over his kitchen to prepare a regional meal but so far they are not telling him what it is.

"We suggested quail, elk and buffalo and certified Hereford beef. I would imagine that one or another of those things might be served, but I just don't know, and if I did know I probably wouldn't be able to tell you," Arnold said.
He said Yeltsin, who onced served Clinton moose lips, should probably stick to the buffalo meat.
"He's had a heart bypass as have I, and he would be very wise to eat buffalo because it's only 2 percent fat instead of the 30 percent fat that beef is," Arnold said.
